Beleza, Andy Abel, Jeff Frankel, me</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today is the nation’s 250</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> anniversary. And it should be a day of celebration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it won’t be. America’s 250</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> birthday will be a grim, glum affair. As far as I can tell, even MAGA enthusiasts are feeling depressed. They certainly aren’t turning out to visit Donald Trump’s sad, shabby state fair.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s a huge difference from the bicentennial, which I celebrated in an unusual but deeply memorable way.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You see, I spent the summer of 1976 in Portugal, which had had its own revolution (the Carnation Revolution) just two years earlier. That revolution overthrew the nation’s fascist dictatorship and created what has proved an enduring democracy.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was there as part of a group of MIT graduate students working at the Banco de Portugal — the country’s equivalent of the Federal Reserve. And I spent the 4</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> at a picnic in a Lisbon park, thrown by the U.S. embassy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It was a small affair. These days Lisbon is overrun with American tourists and expats, but back then there were very few of us around. Even the U.S. government had relatively few people there, because it was trying to keep a low profile in the face of widespread anti-Americanism: Many Portuguese at the time were still talking about how the U.S. had helped overthrow a democratically elected government in Chile three years earlier. There were graffiti around Lisbon saying “Morte à CIA” — although some of these had had “e ao KGB” added in fresher paint.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So the embassy filled out the picnic by inviting Americans it knew were in Lisbon along with staff from other friendly embassies. I remember chatting with a number of West Germans.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The picnic was a charming affair. We stood around munching hot dogs — God knows how they managed that in the land of salt cod and grilled sardines — and listened as the ambassador read a patriotic message from Gerald Ford. And I remember feeling very good about America.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Furthermore, I wasn’t the only American feeling cheerful at the bicentennial, which was somehow an uplifting occasion.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This sunniness may seem odd, given that the U.S. was troubled in many ways. We had just suffered a humiliating defeat in Vietnam. Our cities were a mess: New York had 1600 murders in 1976, more than 5 times the rate last year, and Times Square was an eyesore of drug addicts and porn shops. Oh, and the city had recently gone bankrupt.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet somehow Americans managed to have fun at the bicentennial festivities, and there was a surprising amount of optimism in the air.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One source of optimism was surely the end of the Vietnam War. Yes, it ended in defeat. But it did end, which meant that young Americans and their families no longer had to worry about the draft, and that the nightly news didn’t keep reporting on body counts.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Another source of optimism — something people like JD Vance will never understand — was the fall of Richard Nixon. Satisfaction about how Watergate brought Nixon down wasn’t mainly about partisanship. Instead, the Watergate saga felt like an affirmation of the American spirit. Reporters were heroes and the media did its job. So did Congress. Nobody would call Gerald Ford a great president, but he was clearly a decent human being. The powerful were held accountable. America, it seemed, still retained its soul.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Who would say that now?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the eve of America’s 250</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> birthday we had confirmation of presidential corruption on a scale Nixon could never have imagined. That’s bad in itself. What’s worse is that nobody believes that there will be any consequences for Trump, his cronies, and their henchmen. In 1974 Republicans joined with Democrats to hold Nixon accountable. This time around they’re fully invested in magnifying Trump’s power and his cult of personality, despite knowing perfectly well who he is and what he is doing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;">I am not giving up hope. America is not irretrievably lost. But now, much more than 50 years ago, we are a nation in desperate need of redemption.</p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. That among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.’ It’s operational. Believe me.” — Daniel Inouye</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">China’s last imperial dynasty, the Qing, lasted 268 years. The Ming Dynasty that preceded it lasted just slightly longer, at 276, while the celebrated Tang made it to 289. Decades before each of those dynasties officially fell, they were shells of their former selves, with much of the land outside the control of the central government. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Barring abrupt catastrophe, the United States — which today marks a quarter of a millennium — will probably last as long as the Qing, the Ming, and probably the Tang. The country’s foundations are certainly shakier than when I was a child, but we have not yet entered an obvious terminal phase. The economy is still robust — our GDP remains on the smooth upward trend it has been on since we started measuring such things eight decades ago:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" not) build a functional passenger train network, but our AI industry is upending the world. Our health care costs twice as much as that of other rich nations, but our houses are huge and luxurious. Our cities are burdened with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6fba59b8-64bc-4ffa-a039-9b1cd6f788be?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">crime and disorder</a><span>, but e-commerce delivers everything we need, straight to our door. The hour of the wolf is not yet upon us. It seems a safe bet that there will still be a United States of America in 2044, 2052, and probably 2065. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And yet we’ve reached the stage where we can peer through the fog and see how this grand experiment might be heading toward its conclusion. Much of the country has eased into </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9baa9864-2d08-497f-8205-35a075f13dce?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a comfortable equilibrium of sclerosis</a><span>; local veto power either prevents the construction of factories, housing, energy, transportation, and other infrastructure, or delays it by decades, or raises the cost to multiples of what other rich countries pay. The past has become more valuable than the future to many Americans; they cling desperately to the power to enforce stasis, preserving a facade of the country they grew up in at the expense of the very dynamism that made that country great. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That sclerosis seeps into everything else. Immigration, and even migration from city to city, becomes a vicious zero-sum fight over a fixed housing supply. Cities decay into museums of themselves. The industries of the future can only be built in America if they take up nearly no land, use nearly no energy, require very little bank financing, and are able to procure skilled labor as needed from abroad. Somehow the internet industry satisfied all of those conditions for three decades, but that time is done. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Our politics, meanwhile, has degenerated into movements defined more by who they hate than by any positive vision for the country’s future. Rightists are consumed by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/50f56542-4b4f-4b10-9b27-a3f4cee8d3a1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">their hatred for immigration</a><span>, leftists by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7f6b0f11-f918-4328-9f9f-cb095476dfd1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">their hatred for Israel</a><span>. Even intellectual liberals — my own movement and social class, if only by process of elimination — increasingly subordinate other goals to their dream of lowering the social status of wealthy technologists. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To the extent that popular visions of a better America exist, they are rank and obvious fantasies — homogeneous harmony that rightists </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c043febb-96de-4dee-a55d-cb131a62274e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">will never be able to create</a><span>, or socialist plenty that socialism is incapable of delivering. There are plenty of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b3a38a2-5c00-459d-8d09-01e39a9796a7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">workable, </a><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b3a38a2-5c00-459d-8d09-01e39a9796a7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">feasible</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b3a38a2-5c00-459d-8d09-01e39a9796a7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> future visions</a><span> that would advance the frontiers of freedom, dignity, and prosperity; no faction of the engaged American public seems particularly interested in them. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Political discourse in America is still the baleful thing it became in the 2010s — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a341ec98-7e3d-449f-bff1-18d6a4bbfa2f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a vicious free-for-all of social media influencers</a><span> using hatred, division, fear, and misinformation to win the ear of the powerful political staffer, think tank, and journalist classes. Everything exists in the shadow of the almost-revolution of the late 2010s — an upheaval whose force </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/598a9dda-50ae-4cc4-ba20-28563bb4d2e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">has mostly receded</a><span> but whose damage has yet to be fully assessed. Meanwhile, the country’s powerful enemies abroad are sharpening their knives. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If there is a reason to be pessimistic about America’s future, it’s that so few of the country’s citizens seem to believe in it. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rightists who now dominate the GOP believe that America will only be valuable as a going concern if its old ethnic composition can be forcibly restored. The leftists who are surging among the Democrats, meanwhile, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/67e32dff-f12d-4c5f-90a7-76cd6b904342?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">have a vision of America</a><span> as an evil empire that could have come straight from old Soviet propaganda; this idea finds fertile ground among progressives who for a decade have mainlined the notion that America is “stamped from the beginning” with racism. How will the country be saved if no one thinks it’s something worth saving?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It would be foolish, of course, to predict that the U.S. is headed for the scrap heap within our lifetimes; uncountably many such predictions have made fools of the people who made them. The country is not facing mortal, imminent danger; its enemies are powerful but most of its wounds are self-inflicted. The United States may yet survive, with its territory and its constitutional democracy intact, to its 300th birthday and beyond. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even so, it’s far from clear what a nation will even </span><em>mean</em><span> in those decades and centuries to come. The human race as a whole is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/58c5d1ae-3d7f-4cb8-a6a0-dcf21e63647f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">set to dwindle</a><span>, as fertility falls below replacement in every corner of the globe. At the same time, more and more of the thinking done on the planet </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8ed623a6-7cc6-4a4d-930e-628a9c17af05?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">will be done in data centers</a><span> rather than within human brains. In that posthuman world, it’s not at all clear that humanity will even need the nation-state to provide the crucial organizing and coordinating role it played during the previous two and a half centuries. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So whether or not this is the beginning of the end for America, it’s the beginning of the end for something even bigger and more important — the human age. By that I mean the age when humanity, unassisted by any higher intelligence, broke free of the chains that had bound it for millennia and became something greater.</p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For most of its history, the human race existed at near-animal levels of subsistence. The adoption of agriculture — the most important change in human society before the modern age — increased humanity’s numbers and changed the surface of the Earth, but for the most part it did not alter the species’ fundamental poverty. Civilizations would rise and be cast down again and again by the Malthusian Ceiling. Rome, the Han Dynasty, the Abbasid Caliphate, the Song Dynasty, and many others found themselves unable to outrun what seemed like a fundamental fact of the Universe. And so human existence seemed to be a cycle of rise and fall.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then </span><em>something happened that had never happened before</em><span>. Yes, it’s this:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Humanity became godlike in its powers, blanketing and transforming the globe. And our species achieved this breakout simply by </span><em>coming up with better ideas</em><span> — novel ways to organize ourselves, conduct our affairs, and understand the world around us.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That age of human flowering was remarkably coterminous with the age during which the United States of America was the foremost nation upon the face of the Earth. Or one of the two, I should say, since its only rival for that title was Great Britain. The UK gave birth to industrial technology, modern science, physics, economics, computer science, and so on. But even so, America didn’t just scale up European innovations during its first century. It was at the forefront of innovation from the start — Americans created interchangeable parts, mechanized farm machinery, the telegraph, vulcanized rubber, anesthesia, commercial petroleum drilling, and more. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it was in the late 19th and 20th centuries that America pulled ahead and eclipsed both Great Britain and all other nations of Earth. </span><em>technological</em><span> innovation, the switchover happened around the same time. Over the next few decades, Americans would go on to invent (or co-invent) the telephone, the light bulb, electric power and power grids, skyscrapers, electric motors, air conditioning, airplanes, synthetic plastic, assembly lines, television, FM radio, synthetic fibers, the helicopter, and so on. After World War 2, of course, this dominance became absolute, and America — sometimes together with its allies, sometimes not — invented much of what you see around you in the modern world. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What allowed America both to create this tremendous bounty of innovation, and to spread its economic benefits to the average citizen, was its economic system. The U.S. was always a haven of free enterprise, and markets had much to do with why America was both so innovative and so rich. But it wasn’t the only piece of the puzzle; universal public education, massive government support for infrastructure, the modern university, and government promotion of science all played important roles.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s not clear how much America’s social and governmental innovations — democracy, constitutionalism, federalism, and so on — played a role in enabling and supporting its economic innovations. That’s a question people will be debating for a very long time. But it’s clear that these ideas have become compelling in their own right — almost every country has a constitution, and even dictatorships try to boost their popularity by </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c799c50-701c-4699-85bd-a6de3f6dbc10?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">calling</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c799c50-701c-4699-85bd-a6de3f6dbc10?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> themselves democracies</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And in the </span><em>moral</em><span> realm, the U.S. was almost always at the forefront (depending, of course, on your opinion of what constitutes the “forefront”). Whether it was declaring that “all men are created equal” at its outset, fighting a civil war to end slavery, or pushing the world to accept the idea of universal human rights after World War 2, American ideals often became global ideals with a lag. People also forget how the U.S. pushed European countries — especially </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/25adfb82-950d-4651-9549-798e0ca31070?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the UK</a><span>, but also France and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e99af04a-b015-4d97-b35c-06f2f0cb285a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the Netherlands</a><span> — to give up their colonial empires, using World War 2 and Cold War assistance as leverage. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It is astonishing that </span><em>one single nation</em><span> managed to be at the forefront of the world economically, technologically, institutionally, and morally for well over a century. It is even more astonishing that one nation managed to do all of that during the greatest period of change that humanity had ever known. Wave after wave of wrenching change battered the human race for a quarter of a millennium, and each time, the United States was there, channeling and ultimately mastering the wave before anyone (or almost anyone) else did. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It is common to compare America to great nations or empires of the past. The Rome comparison is the most common, and I started this post by comparing us to imperial China. In fact, these comparisons don’t do justice to what the United States accomplished. Rome, the Song Dynasty, and every other great premodern civilization existed during an essentially static world — the long pause of the agricultural age. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The United States has spent its entire quarter millennium of existence in the chaos following the Industrial Revolution. It survived a 250-year period that saw the end of the British Empire, the Russian Empire, the Qing Dynasty, the Japanese Empire, the French Empire, the Soviet Union, and countless other regimes. But it didn’t just survive for that whole 250 years; it </span><em>led the world</em><span> in </span><em>almost all respects</em><span> during most of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s the most incredible performance of any country in human history so far. Even if you count all 5000 years of Chinese history as one single country, just 250 years of America managed to eclipse that totality in many ways.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">How did America pull this off? Its populace was large, but smaller than China, India, or the old USSR. It had a lot of natural resources, but the British Empire, Russia, and the Qing Dynasty had just as many. Its people were not more intelligent or harder-working or inherently more moral. Christianity did not produce similar results elsewhere. What was America’s secret sauce?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s possible, of course, that the United States simply lucked out from an extended sequence of right-places-at-the-right-times. But although we’ll never know, I suspect that America’s secret sauce was </span><em>respect for the human individual</em><span>.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The system of free enterprise that allowed the U.S. economy to flourish was based on the idea of giving individuals free rein to pursue financial gain within the boundaries of the law. The democracy and human rights that the U.S. championed were both based on respect for the individual, and other countries adopted these ideas when they found that their populaces demanded them. Individualism made it difficult for the U.S. to get captured by the kind of totalitarianism that captured Germany, Russia, and many other countries during the turbulent 20th century. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As for that large population, the entire reason that America has a large population is </span><em>immigration</em><span>. There has always been a loud minority of Americans who declared that people from poorer countries — “beaten men from beaten races”, as Francis Walker wrote in 1896 — weren’t collectively fit to become Americans, and that their presence would destroy the country. But America’s deep-rooted institutional respect for the individual kept the immigration flowing, which eventually gave the country its large population, large domestic market, deep fiscal pockets, and huge talent pool. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is why the American age was the human age. The United States represented a living demonstration that if the institutions of society placed the value of the human individual above all else, then individuals would serve society to the best of their abilities. This does not mean that the group or collective was unimportant; it means that the collective is the most powerful when uplifting, empowering, and respecting the individual is its goal. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That, I believe, is the true meaning of “All men are created equal” — the most important 5 words ever written. It does not mean that all humans are equally strong, or smart, or good. It means that the inherent value of a human comes not from their capabilities, but from their individuality. The United States certainly never embodied this ideal to perfection, but the principle did the country, and the world, great service nonetheless.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whether this principle will continue to produce the best societies in the world remains an open question. There are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c6a1f73b-5a84-4b2f-bd7c-f1d6ef050f48?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">serious reasons to question</a><span> whether the primacy of the individual was a form of organization </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/76d44f9a-1458-4905-9b73-1901f682eac9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">suited only to a particular time</a><span> in the history of technology. Social media collapses independent thought, which can destroy the “wisdom of crowds”. AI provides an information aggregation decision-making mechanism that might one day eclipse markets, democracy, and other systems based on collections of independent human individuals. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s conceivable, in other words, that in the posthuman age, countries like America will not only lose their edge, but their whole reason for existence. Human rights, democracy, free enterprise, and so on might turn out to be ephemeral, transitional arrangements — shady pavilions under which intelligent life on Earth took a brief rest before continuing on to bigger and much weirder things. Or it might turn out that there are deep reasons, as yet poorly understood, why respect for the individual may always turn out to be the best way to organize society. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Regardless, I think it’s important that we acknowledge the singular importance and success of the United States of America during humanity’s most heroic age. It may last 1000 more years, or just 10, but it has already earned its place as the greatest country in history. </p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: major news except for all the other disasters happening, Donald Trump has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fed4ba54-4fb2-4c38-bbff-7f06d44c1ae3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">declined to renew the USMCA</a><span> — the successor to the North American Free Trade Agreement — which he himself negotiated. This puts businesses on notice that tariff-free shipments within North America, which NAFTA supposedly made permanent, may go away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Some commentators have dismissed this as no big deal, because Trump’s successor will probably reverse his decision and make the USMCA permanent after all. However, this misses the point of such agreements. Before NAFTA went into effect, North American tariffs were already low. The average tariff imposed by the US on imports from Mexico was only 2 percent. But NAFTA gave more than tariff relief. It gave, or seemed to give, certainty: businesses could invest in border-spanning supply chains confident that they would be able to use these chains for many years to come.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Or, as it turns out, not, if we have a U.S. president who doesn’t care about breaking promises.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Bloomberg ran a segment about all of this, with a substantial part coming from an interview I had with David Westin a few weeks ago:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c0bb27a0-7dce-4512-b9bb-9e96dee870fd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/nIhm4sqmOkc" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Transcript</strong><span>:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin </span></strong><span>We start with the poster child for North American trade, the auto industry. Since the USMCA’s predecessor, NAFTA, came into effect over 30 years ago, autos have been at the center of negotiations. The reason is simple. The industry is tightly integrated across northern and southern US borders, borders like the one between Detroit, Michigan and Windsor, Ontario. This is the brand new Gordie Howe International Bridge that spans the Detroit River, separating the Motor City from Windsor. It was named for the famed hockey player who was born in Canada but crossed the border to lead the Detroit Red Wings to four Stanley Cups. Canada paid for the bridge, but now President Trump has put its opening on hold, which in itself is unlikely to divide the two cities’ economies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>Those are not really separate cities. There just happens to be a borderline through them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin </span></strong><span>Economist Paul Krugman won the Nobel Prize for his work on trade.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>Stuff does go back and forth. There’s a tremendous amount of specialization, which is good for everybody. It reduces costs, increases efficiency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin: </span></strong><span>One of the companies benefiting from that back and forth trade is Linamar, a manufacturer with headquarters outside of Toronto. Jim Jarrell is its CEO.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jarrell </span></strong><span>So we’re 60 years old and really I think when you look at Linamar, we’re an advanced manufacturing and product design technology company with 37,000 people global, 87 facilities around the world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin:</span></strong><span> When we talk about the auto part of Linamar’s business, how much of your production goes across either the Canadian-U.S. border or the U.S.-Mexican border or for that matter Canada-Mexico?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jarrell </span></strong><span>I would say a ton. There is so much interconnection, integration between it. And I think we’ve demonstrated this before. We have one part that we do for an OEM customer, two OEMs in the U.S. and the original part that we get is a forging that comes into Mexico, which goes into the U.S. to get some further processing, comes into Canada for further processing, back to the U.S. for further processing, over to Canada where we do the sort of final assembly, and then that gets distributed back into the U.S.as well as Mexico and Canadian auto plants. So again, you can see this full integration Of this, you know, supply chain in the automotive North American area. And one thing we say is you can’t unbake the omelet, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Manufacturing has become a regional game.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin:</span></strong><span> Shannon O’Neil is the director of studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, author of the book, “The Globalization Myth, Why Regions Matter,” and a Bloomberg opinion contributor.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>O’Neil </span></strong><span>The strength, frankly, of the U.S. auto industry is really a North American auto industry. It is that because cars and car parts are produced across Mexico, Canada, and the United States, they are strong, they are competitive and they’re affordably priced. And it’s that connection, those supply chains across North America that are important for autos. important for all kinds of manufacturing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin:</span></strong><span> Given how the, I’ll call it, North American auto industry has evolved, is it even possible to cut off imports and exports of automobiles and auto parts between the United States and Canada and/or Mexico?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>O’Neil </span></strong><span>There’s a real question if we didn’t have NAFTA, if we didn’t have USMCA, would we have a North American car industry at all, if we didn’t have the economies of scale of production that have now developed over North America? Could we bring back just a U.S.-produced car? Sure, we could, but it would be a much more expensive car. It would likely be a less innovative car in terms of the parts that go into it. And it would be really hard to compete against imports from Japan, South Korea, Europe,and other places.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin: </span></strong><span>The USMCA may have been a win-win for auto industry companies like Linamar and for American consumers, but it hasn’t necessarily addressed President Trump’s underlying concerns about the balance of trade between the U.S. and either Canada or Mexico. For 2025, the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico was nearly $200 billion, with Canada about $46 billion. But O’Neill says regardless of the trade deficit, President Trump is underestimating the extent to which the U.S. needs trade both ways with both Canada and Mexico.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jarrell </span></strong><span>What we see is a big influx of goods coming from Mexico to the United States. It’s now the number one exporter to the United States, or U.S. importer. In part, that’s replacing Chinese trade. In part, that is just the strength of North American supply chains and the back and forth of goods and services that move there. But we also need to remember that Mexico and Canada are the number one export markets for U.S. companies, for U.S. products that go out into the world. So we are very dependent on them as they are on us.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: Another concern often expressed by President Trump when it comes to trade, particularly in the auto industry, is the loss of jobs, something Krugman admits is real, but not really the fault of the USMCA. What do you say to people from my home state of Michigan who hear President Trump say, you know, that’s a good idea? We’re going to actually have some barriers put up so that we have more of those plants in Michigan, in Ohio, so we have better jobs? Because we have lost a lot of those jobs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>We have lost a lot of jobs, but it’s not mostly because of NAFTA, right? I still call it NAFTA, sorry, it’s a lot easier given that Trump keeps changing the name. But anyway, do we have fewer manufacturing jobs in the United States, do we have fewer auto jobs in the United States because of the USMCA? I think that’s highly doubtful. The idea that somehow turning our back on the world here is going to add jobs is probably wrong.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: And then there’s China, not part of USMCA negotiations, but always a specter in the room.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>China is looming over all of these negotiations and this real worry about China selling products into the United States using Mexico or Canada as a backdoor in, right, getting the benefits of free trade without actually being party to the negotiations and to the agreements. And so what we’ve seen is Mexico in particular push back against Chinese imports, which have grown dramatically over the last five years into Mexico. Some of this are cars and car parts and the like, some are other electronics and the like. So we’ve seen them push back to really support North America. And as we get into the USMCA negotiations, China and this idea of transshipment, of shipping parts in through Mexico to the United States, is a big part of the conversation. And one can see, and I think all parties are open to, creating a real North America fortress vis-a-vis China, vis-a-vis other imports from around the world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re in a world now where, as we’ve seen, interdependence can be weaponized. We used to think that that was something we did to other countries, but now we find out that other countries do it to us, too. So the idea that you need to maintain capacity in your own country or in reliable allies for strategically important stuff is now very, very real. I am really reluctant to be where I am right now, but I do think that conditional tariffs on Chinese cars are probably going to be necessary. I don’t think that the Europeans can allow their auto industry to be totally hollowed out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, there’s some compromise here. Probably totally trying to shut Chinese cars out of the market is going to be a bad thing, be very costly to consumers. But on the other hand, I’ve been shocked not only by my own change of mind, but by some of my colleagues, people who are longtime advocates of globalization and free trade who are saying, okay, Europe needs to do some, really, if you like, it’s national security, it’s market disruption, to just allow something as big as the European auto industry to just be overrun, even if consumers would benefit for a while, it’s not 20 years ago anymore. We really do need to rethink, which is a long way from saying that we should have tariffs on everything or that the Europeans should have tariffs on everything. But a much more interventionist position has become really hard to avoid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: But for all the concern about trade deficits and jobs and putting sand in the gears of the North American auto industry, those most closely involved have one concern above all. I would say certainty has got to be the prize award that we’ve got to be chasing here. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>I just think that is absolutely critical to have that. The great virtue of this whole world’s trade system that the United States basically set up after World War II was that it provided, it wasn’t just that their tariffs were low, though that’s important, but even more important, things were predictable. I would almost prefer that Trump put on more tariffs on Canada and Mexico, but committed to keep them in place, than have rolling negotiations where every year you don’t know what next year will be like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: If you were advising President Trump how to win the negotiation with Canada and Mexico, what would you advise him?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>The USMCA is an easy case because this is not, there is no trade conflict here except in Trump’s mind. All of the things we’re talking about are not a problem for the USMCA. We shouldn’t be worried about being dependent on Canadian aluminum. They’ve got the hydropower, they’ve got the cheap electricity, they’re right next to us. They speak almost the same language. This is not an issue. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We are not really worried about the U.S. auto industry being hollowed out by Mexican auto production because Mexican auto production is part of an integrated system, which actually probably makes the U.S. more competitive. No, the USMCA, or maybe just rename it NAFTA and go back to the original purpose, which is this is a case where it really makes sense to have a true free trade area. In fact, if I could, I would say this is a case where we should go beyond free trade to a European Union style customs union with free movement of goods across borders, no checks at all, a common external frontier for goods. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>We have a real problem with China. The problem with Mexico and Canada is just a figment of the president’s imagination.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/706d4a66-46dc-495e-8e36-be89dabbcf7d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Joe Raedle</a><span>/Staff via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Almost all of the questions today were about Democrats’ ongoing tea party moment in primaries, which got me thinking about the actual Tea Party of the Obama years. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the time, the Tea Party talked an enormous amount about government spending and budget deficits,</span><strong> </strong><span>and mainstream Republicans largely treated it as a movement about fiscal conservatism. A desire to harness Tea Party energy was part of why Mitt Romney picked Paul Ryan as his running mate and challenged Obama on a platform of steep spending cuts rather than Moderate Massachusetts Mitt pragmatism. Around this time, I worked with Vanessa Williamson’s husband and I knew Theda Skocpol from college, so I was aware of the book the two of them wrote in 2013 called “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/df2f4da4-5a8a-4d97-800b-1c8205acabc2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>The Tea Party and the Remaking of Republican Conservatism</span></a><span>.” It was a sociological deep dive into Tea Party activism and featured the striking and contrarian claim that </span><em><span>actually</span></em><span> the number one issue motivating the movement was immigration. Very few people in 2013 agreed with that, but after watching Donald Trump’s 2016 primary win, I think everyone familiar with this literature reached the conclusion that Williamson and Skocpol were right all along. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I raise this because, while we’ve had a ton of takes about what is driving the restive left on the Democratic side, I </span><em><span>don’t</span></em><span> think we’ve had anything equivalent to </span><span>Williamson and Skocpol in the sense of a genuinely good-faith, curiosity-motivated look at what’s going on. This is not to say I have my own secret theory. I also don’t want to overread the analogy. Just because the Tea Party seemed to be about one thing and turned out to be about another doesn’t mean the left insurgency is like that. It may just be that it’s actually a bad analogy. But I do want to draw the distinction between disinterested scholarly inquiry and factional or partisan combat. A lot of influential figures in right-wing politics really wanted it to be the case that the Tea Party was about widespread demand for entitlement cuts, and they successfully imposed that interpretation on the world for a period of years until it all blew up in their face. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-5f7?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=284361510" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>lindamc:</span></a><span> I’m a Common Sense Dem at the end of my tether. I split my time between DC, with an incoming socialist mayor, and Ann Arbor MI, where socialists are seeking to unseat the local government that has (as noted in a recent mailbag) finally started building here. Everyone knows about the Senate race 😩. Many/most youngs I know are self-described socialists with little/no understanding of what that means in historic terms, and the overwhelming majority of my fellow olds are Heather Cox Richardsonians. Virtually every social gathering I attend features someone making a glib, ignorant complaint about data centers. A “swing dancing in the park” event I attended a few days ago started out with pronouns and cultural appropriation and never made it to demonstrating actual dance steps. Things seem to somehow get worse and worse.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>How do you cope with this? Despite fighting hard against it, I feel something like actual despair a lot of the time.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m feeling a little bit untethered myself this summer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But one thing that I try to remind myself of is that a lot of what I am experiencing ambiently is not so much a real political trend as the output of the extraordinary New York-centricity of the national media. </span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Imagine if the whole national press were concentrated in San Francisco. You’d have stories talking about how Dan Lurie is the most popular mayor in America. But they’d also be talking about how his successes were really prefigured by Brooke Jenkins. And about how part of why both Lurie and Jenkins are succeeding is that they belong to a broader reform faction in San Francisco politics that’s winning Board of Supervisors races and contesting internal Democratic Party offices and poised to make a run at the school board. You’d see Matt Mahan down the road in San Jose. You’d talk about how his gubernatorial bid fizzled, but you’d also know Tom Steyer’s leftist gubernatorial bid fizzled, too. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And if the press were a little less New York-centric, we’d hear more about Chicago, too: The left won power there, and it’s been an embarrassing failure they don’t talk about anymore.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An electoral backlash to Mayor Brandon Johnson is clearly coming, and the only real question is whether it will be a retreat to status quo mainstream Democratic governance or if we’ll see a more dramatic form of pushback. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fbfe894b-e9bc-40f8-b7bd-808d7d9221d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>A City That Works</span></a><span>, which began as a Chicago-focused Substack very much aligned with Slow Boring values, has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/914ca6df-bcfd-496b-bb40-daeed9cf2724?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>now launched a PAC</span></a><span> that is going to try to get not just a good mayor but some good City Council members elected to bring some of the San Francisco magic to the Windy City. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From a D.C. perspective, I am sad that Kenyan McDuffie lost. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it’s possible that the only way to move forward from where D.C. was under Muriel Bowser’s third term was to take this detour. Voters in the city wanted change, and McDuffie read as continuity. Something I tried to say to people (mostly unsuccessfully) is that the direction of change matters. But now that there’s been a regime change in the city, the opening exists to articulate a smart reformist critique of the status quo and to find some outsider figures to run for office on a smart program. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even in New York, where a lot of attention has been paid to Darializa Avila Chevalier’s continued advocacy for prison abolition, it’s clear that Zohran Mamdani understands perfectly well that a successful mayor needs a safe city. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As someone who was engaged in a lot of very nasty disputes about policing in the summer of 2020, I am personally </span><em><span>extremely</span></em><span> annoyed that the left’s surrender on this has taken the form of acting peevish about anyone raising their old tweets. I would love for someone to write on the internet, “You know what, I disagree with Matt Yglesias about a lot of things, but not only was he correct about police defunding, he was gutsy to say so at a time when it was controversial.” To the best of my knowledge, nobody at all has ever done that even as virtually the whole left has moved toward my view. So I’m aggravated about the situation and I find the discourse — especially in N.Y.C.-centric media — to be fairly despair-inducing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But while the situation is somewhat grave, that’s mostly just because politics is important and the stakes always feel high. The actual trends across the country are fairly mixed and there are reasons for both optimism and pessimism. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Where I do give the left credit is on two related points where I think there are valuable lessons to be learned. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One is that they have real team spirit. Bernie Sanders has been tireless and fairly selfless in touring the country to elevate the profile of Bernie-aligned candidates and help them raise money. Then his more successful acolytes like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pay it forward and do the same. And even the different members of this movement </span><em><span>say they are members of a movement</span></em><span> rather than insisting that each one is a beautiful unique snowflake. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other point is that they are not terrified of losing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s easy to imagine a world where Graham Platner’s campaign ended up looking like an embarrassing failure rather than a striking success. And Steyer’s campaign really was an embarrassing failure. But having failed in an embarrassing way with Steyer, they just moved on to some wins in New York and then talked a lot about those wins. I know people who were involved in directing money to Baldacci and then immediately felt like they were in hot water for being involved in something that failed. But the fact is that he came very close to winning his primary and he was the right candidate. It’s too bad that more wasn’t done to support him (and that he’s not more mediagenic), but you need to try things. And you need to have some grace for people who try things and it doesn’t work out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-5f7?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=284461831" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">lwdlyndale:</a><span> The Times finally decided to write something </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/94b7fb25-cf2d-4d22-b366-719ad6b4208b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">about Andy Beshear and his bid for the White House</a><span>: Do you think there’s any chance we could see some real #Andymentum in the 2028 cycle, or do you think, like most of the chattering classes, that he’s obviously doomed?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On the subject of trying things, I think the problem with Beshear-type politicians is that they are excessively risk-averse. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a level where, yes, Beshear seems like a strong candidate on paper, especially for primary voters who say electability is their top priority. But to beat Republicans, he needs the nomination first. So the easy strategy is to just emphasize his winning credentials in a non-specific way and say he’s not a far-left socialist but also not say anything that could alienate any mainstream Democrats whose support he needs. The problem with this is that it’s boring and indistinct and vague and ultimately leaves him with no firm footing when inevitable misfortunes come his way. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An alternative strategy would be to:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Pick some positions that are popular with the median voter in Kentucky but unpopular with most Democratic Party elected officials. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Articulate those positions clearly and say they make you a different kind of Democrat and that’s why you can win nationally. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Make the case that the path to progressive goals is to be a 50-state party that can expand Medicaid, crush MAGA, and enact big durable change in the country. </p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This will probably not work! The odds are good that step one just kills you. But it </span><em>might</em><span> work. If he tried it, I would say nice things about him. And so would other people. And some others would say mean things about him. And there would be a proper argument about it. The problem is that if you’re Beshear, the default strategy might be to run a lame campaign that stirs no controversy and fails for obvious reasons but sets you up for a cabinet job. What I want to see is him try a higher variance strategy where he really explains what people in Kentucky think and care about and where he challenges presidential primary voters to care about winning in places like that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-5f7?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=284397673" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Jesse Ewiak:</a><span> It’s the day after Election Day in 2026.</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Graham Platner has won by 6 to 7 points.</strong></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Abdul El-Sayed has won by 3 to 4 points.</strong></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>How cooked is the moderate wing in the upcoming 2028 primaries and should they just put their power behind somebody like Ossoff instead of attempting to slam Shapiro or someone similar through the primaries?</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think this is the wrong way to think about it. What is “the moderate wing” at this point, really? To me the worst way to think about 2028 is to start with the idea that there’s A.O.C. and everyone else is “moderate,” so Democrats need to try our hardest to elect a moderate (i.e. not A.O.C.) and therefore decide if we should get behind Shapiro or Newsom or Ossoff or who. What I want to do is start with the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe4e582c-89ce-43ea-a738-8f74999b6c00?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">values of the Common Sense Democrat Manifesto</a><span> and then back whichever candidate best embodies those values. I am open to that person being Shapiro or Ossoff or someone else or even A.O.C. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I want to be a policy demander and see some elements of the field try to move toward my views. </p><p class="button-wrapper" href="https://substack.com/redirect/9ce27e0f-f0ac-42ec-a194-aefa62d2e721?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>ranking Biden’s mistakes</span></a><span> and wanting to discredit Bidenism. This made me wonder what Biden got right (an admittedly short list) that Matt’s would want to see replicated in Democratic politics.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Biden got a lot of things right in the sense that I agree with his position on abortion rights and I think it’s correct to enforce the Clean Air Act rather than </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2d856d3c-4291-4064-a50d-6a882e31ca5e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">try to bring back coal</a><span>. I thought both the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and the clean-energy-production tax credits in the Inflation Reduction Act were good ideas. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I think the spirit of the question is more what did Biden bring to the table distinctively that Democrats writ large should learn from. And here I think it’s not that much. Criticisms of Biden’s handling of the Israel/Gaza conflict are so over the top that I count as a defender of the administration — I just do not think it’s true that they were complicit in the perpetration of a genocide. And unlike Trump, they were able to avoid getting dragged into a war with Iran. But if you think about the administration’s policy goals as of October 8, 2023, they did not succeed. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Elsewhere in foreign policy, though, I think Biden was more successful. His Ukraine policy basically worked. The various export controls related to A.I. were good and involved a fair amount of deft diplomatic work. To me it’s a shame that the conventional wisdom is to shrink all of foreign policy down to Israel and then condemn the Biden team for failing to bring the world’s most famously intractable conflict to a satisfactory resolution. Biden was, by background and inclination, a guy who was most knowledgeable about foreign affairs and most interested in foreign affairs, and he did his best work in that area. Withdrawing from Afghanistan, for example, though politically costly, was the correct call. Even if it was not executed perfectly, it was executed much better than the previous 20 years of war. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On domestic issues, it’s not that it was all bad. It’s that it wasn’t really Biden’s focus, so he was mostly just going along with the consensus. This led to an egregious failure around immigration, because the consensus was kind of incoherent, and insofar as the economic ideas differed from Bill Clinton or Barack Obama they were worse.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6d8750e5-65d6-4604-9b5e-58632d32cfb0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>City of Trees:</span></a><span> Why isn’t rent seeking as captivating to people who think that things are rigged against society? To me, it seems like a very straightforward case of government and businesses colluding with each other to enrich the rent seekers at the expense of the citizens. But it doesn’t seem to motivate as much as more complex conspiracy theories, accusations of concentrated corporate power, or the like. I have some guesses of my own, but what’s your take?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Rent-seeking” itself is, obviously, a kind of technical term that is not likely to capture people’s imagination. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I agree that it seems like there should potentially be a politics in saying “nefarious forces are using political power to rig the economy and make you worse off” and then instead of naming fake stuff you name the real stuff. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A partial answer is that by far the most economically consequential form of rent-seeking is in the real estate market and there actually is a pretty robust YIMBY movement in the United States that is winning some elections and passing some laws. So I think the question is does what’s worked for YIMBY politics generalize? Here it’s tough because the economic gains from tackling any one non-housing set of rent-seekers is pretty limited. If you take a very right-coded group of rent-seeking interests, like car dealership owners, it’s pretty easy to go viral on Bluesky with a call to crack down on them. But doing actual political organizing against an entrenched lobby is harder and the actual upside of reforming car-dealership-franchise laws is modest. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now if you go bigger and say we’re taking on the car dealers </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cce3515a-b931-443f-8c3a-00c1f2547d58?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>and the dentists</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a52fb76b-0ad2-4e07-af29-007d32e18b55?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>the American Medical Association</span></a><span> and also the Jones Act and promoting port automation and all the rest, then you have substantial political upside. But to do that, you need to be willing to take on interest groups that are not as heavily right-coded, including labor unions. And to do </span><em><span>that</span></em><span> you need to challenge the big-picture conceptual framework that is deeply entrenched on the left, which holds that since 1980 or so, the United States has been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bddfcacc-3371-46ea-af8b-634d254dffa7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>ruled by something called “neoliberalism” that is characterized by helter-skelter deregulation</span></a><span>. In a lot of ways I actually think that’s a bigger barrier than anything more properly structural, like union power. A funny thing about the D.S.A. primary wins is that in almost every case, they are beating solidly progressive Democratic incumbents over the objections of public sector unions. Mamdani doesn’t owe anything at all to New York City labor. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But ideology matters. The people voting for D.S.A. candidates are overwhelmingly not working-class themselves, but they have a very sincere romantic relationship with the </span><em><span>idea</span></em><span> of working-class politics, which involves an </span><em><span>idea</span></em><span> of labor union politics that instinctively rejects the idea that some maritime union whose members probably aren’t even progressive at all is posing bigger problems for average people’s economic well-being than anything Jeff Bezos has ever done. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-5f7?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=284373929" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>srynerson:</span></a><span> Would you support a constitutional amendment to increase House terms to four years, with 50% of the House being up for reelection every two years, so there are still House elections every two years?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m not sure there’s a good word to describe what I want to say here, but there’s a category of reform proposals that strike me as probably a good idea (and thus, in some sense, I support them), but I would really not recommend dedicating any time, money, or mental energy to the cause. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The United States House of Representatives suffers from a very large and worsening problem of partisan gerrymandering. Not only does this cause a lot of direct bad consequences, but it is creating a tendency to turn state elections just into proxy wars over gerrymandering and that’s going to have really bad downstream consequences for the quality of state government. There is also a very straightforward solution to the problem of partisan gerrymandering, namely proportional representation. This would be a heavy lift to get done, but it’s not impossible and it would have big benefits. There are plausible arguments for other reforms and I’m not against them, but I think it’s a bad idea to get distracted by them. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" Immigrants assimilate to American culture, but they also do change that culture somewhat; </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/533eff91-a9a4-4b26-ad78-d54a2d38d0b4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">assimilation is a two-way street</a><span>. It’s impossible to live in the same country you grew up in — technology is still the biggest cause of cultural change — but if you want to preserve as much of the country of your youth as humanly possible, then it makes sense to restrict immigration. More broadly, if you believe that nation-states are legitimate entities, then you must admit that countries have an inherent right to preserve their cultures in amber by shutting themselves off to immigration, if they want to. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But MAGA has already lost that battle. America is not North Korea; we’re not even Japan or Sweden. 79% of Americans say that immigration is good for the country overall; they say this even knowing that immigration will cause some long-term cultural changes. The cultural preservation argument against immigration is a lost cause, no matter how desperately its proponents shriek and bluster and threaten. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">At the same time, Democrats must be extremely wary of embracing open borders simply out of pure reaction to MAGA nativism. Americans don’t want to let just anyone in; they want people to come legally, and they want to admit people who earn enough money to contribute positively to the economy. If Democrats simply respond to each electoral victory by throwing open the borders and turning a blind eye to illegal immigration, the American people will continue to respond by intermittently electing xenophobes. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the age of low fertility, America desperately needs to be </span><em>smart </em><span>about its immigration strategy. underline;">poll</a><span> supposedly showing “socialism gaining ground with young voters.” But I don’t believe it. Young people may be more receptive to the </span><em>word</em><span> socialism, but that’s only because right-wingers constantly use that word to smear policies that have nothing to do with real socialism — i.e., government ownership of the means of production.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The fact is that very few Americans — even among politicians who call themselves “democratic socialists” — are really socialists. What many, I’d say a majority, of Americans support is what Europeans call social democracy — an ideology that is OK with living in a mostly market-driven economic system in which some people make much more money than others, but one that advocates policies to tame markets and inequality with progressive taxation, safety net programs, and regulations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">America already has an extensive range of social-democratic policies, although they are weaker than those in most other rich countries. And sustaining social democracy — indeed, making U.S. social democracy stronger — has very broad support, even among Republicans. Actual socialism, by contrast, has little public appeal.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why, then, does it look as if socialism is on the rise? Mainly because right-wing propagandists continually smear social democratic policies as socialist, trying to make popular, mainstream policy ideas sound extreme. And some Americans who are basically social democrats in effect respond by saying, “Well, if that’s socialism, I guess I’m OK with socialism.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Right-wingers often try to portray social democratic policies as somehow un-American. But social democracy is as American as sliced bread, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a56767f4-01e7-4147-b8a0-5be3dcacc51d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">invented in 1928</a><span>. The Social Security Act, which created a safety net for the disabled and the unemployed as well as retirees, was passed just a few years later, in 1935. A national minimum wage was established in 1938. The big healthcare programs, Medicare and Medicaid, weren’t established until 1965 — but even that was 60 years ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So very few Americans even remember a nation that didn’t have a large, expensive social safety net — albeit one with some big holes in it. (In Texas, 19 percent of the population under 65 and 14 percent of children lack health insurance.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Progressive taxation has also been around for a very long time. When people say that they favor socialism, surely what they are often really saying is that they are angry about the rise of oligarchy. They are </span><em>not</em><span> demanding a dictatorship of the proletariat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>And while there are, of course, left-wing radicals in America, they have no realistic prospect of getting their way. So it’s important to understand what the current uproar over socialism is really about.
