Allegiance at the start of the day. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf00166e-4474-48c6-9266-93bcbcf22f02?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Boston Globe</a><span>/Contributor via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I was at a couple of education events in the spring that all featured very smart, very achievement-oriented people talking about how to address the national crisis in basic reading and math attainment. A common lament was that politicians and pundits are simply not focused enough on the question of whether kids are learning the basics, preferring to fire off hot takes about culture war topics. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a view that I very much sympathize with and have articulated over the years. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That said, I’ve also been in a bunch of conversations about things like Noah Smith’s essay on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da73a801-404e-469c-a7b8-3dab254d38a3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">need for a revival of American liberal nationalism</a><span> or Jerusalem Demsas’s take about how </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/247e7fdd-85b3-4793-92b1-fc866059f2ad?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">you have to love America in order to save it</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I broadly agree with these takes. But I also find that they’re a little bit lacking in specificity. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I know that Rob Sand, who’s running for governor in Iowa, does things like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/522cef80-8b03-4592-8779-144fe3bec2d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">open town halls by having everyone sing “America the Beautiful.”</a><span> A friend described Sand as the Daniel Day-Lewis of politics: He understood quite some time ago that trends in Democratic Party politics were going one way and political trends in Iowa were going another, and he fully committed to a hyper-distinctive post-partisan Iowa-as-fuck persona. He never breaks character, and he not only performs the patriotic ritual, he makes it seem natural. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But if liberals want to embrace American patriotism, that has to mean more than just clicking “like” and “share” on columns that express a second-order thesis that it would be desirable to see more liberal patriotism. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You need to actually do something specific, the way Sand does. I think Democrats should actually do some patriotism.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Pledging allegiance </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a House bill called the “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/53578aa2-474d-4b5b-b2c5-7815b93ed0e4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Promoting American Patriotism In Our Schools Act</a><span>,” which is sponsored by Dale Strong of Alabama and co-sponsored by a handful of other Republicans. It would require public schools receiving federal Elementary and Secondary Education Act funds to “recite the Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America at the beginning of each school day.” It then also, to ensure conformity with free speech law, specifies that students must be allowed to opt out of pledging without penalty. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My (private) K-8 school opened every day with the Pledge of Allegiance, and I later went to a more progressive high school that did not. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This obviously did not make a huge difference in practice, but it does set a different kind of tone. Of course, as a fussy writer and former philosophy student, I’ve always found the idea of pledging allegiance to a </span><em>flag</em><span> a little bit odd. A flag is a symbol of a thing, not a thing. Historically, the design of the flag has changed many times as a result of the accession of new states, and it’s not like people are switching allegiances when the flag changes. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it is what it is. The text says that we are pledging allegiance not just to the flag but also “to the republic for which it stands,” which seems like the important part. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And I think if you’re going to be patriotic, then you ought to be loyal to the American republic. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We’re currently in a funny place where I think if I were to say “Democrats should promote the idea that people should be loyal to the American republic,” that would be considered an incredibly lukewarm take. But it’s not surprising or confusing to anyone that all the sponsors on the pledge bill are Republicans. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet, historically, this pledge to the flag and to the republic for which it stands is the conventional ritual. So isn’t Representative Strong just right about this? Again, I’m not saying students should be hauled into detention for refusing to engage in coerced speech. But most people tend to go along to get along. Defaults matter, and it seems to me that promoting a default of loyalty to the United States of America is a totally reasonable function for a public school system.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I also think that Democrats in particular increasingly need to ask themselves what they think a public school system is for. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Voucherizing the public school system is unpopular, and opposing that is often one of red state Democrats’ best issues. But Democrats struggle to articulate an actual purpose for these public institutions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One such purpose, of course, should be student achievement. But that really has to be achievement at the low end. I don’t think it’s really credible to deny that affluent educated parents could just take the money and secure good education for our own kids. The people who’d be failed by a privatized solution are the kinds of kids who private schools would just try to screen out. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Lifting up students at the low end is an important cause. But I don’t think you can really talk about public education in a clear way without talking about the civic function of schools, and that should include cultivating a positive national identity. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Sweet land of liberty </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Marian Anderson was one of the most famous American singers of the 1930s. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>She was also African American, which greatly impacted her ability to tour and perform in the American South. This reached a head in 1939, when her manager tried to get her booked to perform at Constitution Hall run by the Daughters of the American Revolution here in Washington, D.C. They said no, upholding a color bar against Black performers. The D.C. Board of Education </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2dcc5efa-ea4f-4471-a684-343506e567f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">also denied permission</a><span> to use the Central High School auditorium as a venue. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The N.A.A.C.P. decided to use this as an organizing opportunity and started a big campaign to pressure DAR to let Anderson sing. Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the organization and led thousands of others to join her in doing so. Franklin Roosevelt was legendarily hyper-cautious about embracing civil rights issues, but he was persuaded that this one was a winner and his Interior Secretary Harold Ickes gave permission to organize an open-air concert on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For her first song, Anderson performed “My Country, ‘Tis of Thee,” the one about how America is a sweet land of liberty.  </p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/13e19c03-c05f-465f-813b-ba2960e601e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/mAONYTMf2pk" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The concert was a huge deal, and it’s not a coincidence that 24 years later, Martin Luther King Jr., also speaking from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, closed his “I Have a Dream” speech with the same song: </p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #04B2A5;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This will be the day when all of God’s children will be able to sing with new meaning. “My country, ‘tis of thee, sweet land of liberty, of thee I sing. Land where my fathers died, land of the pilgrim’s pride, from every mountainside, let freedom ring.” And if America is to be a great nation, this must become true. So let freedom ring from the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire. Let freedom ring from the mighty mountains of New York. Let freedom ring from the heightening Alleghenies of Pennsylvania. Let freedom ring from the snow-capped Rockies of Colorado. Let freedom ring from the curvaceous slopes of California. But not only that. Let freedom ring from Stone Mountain of Georgia. Let freedom ring from Lookout Mountain of Tennessee. Let freedom ring from every hill and molehill of Mississippi, from every mountainside. Let freedom ring!</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a conventional progressive point here that true patriots have always worked to improve their country rather than just be complacent about it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I also think it’s worth taking this whole sequence of events seriously. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anderson is singing the song somewhat ironically. Her point was that to a considerable extent, America was in fact </span><em>not</em><span> a land of liberty. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet the performance worked, because people all across the country were taught to sing it non-ironically. Some people probably noticed the mismatch between the stated ideal and the reality; lots of people probably didn’t and just took it at face value. Yet it’s precisely because people grew up sincerely believing that America was a sweet land of liberty that gave the performance its punch. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If everyone had been raised to think of the United States as a country built on stolen land, enslaved labor, and genocide, then there’s actually no dissonance to resolve — a white person would simply think he had a pretty good deal in life.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s clearly a view that’s had a lot of influence over American educational practice that if you tell everyone how terrible everything is, that will inspire them to be activists for change. But most people just don’t care that much about politics and never will — you’re just fostering cynicism, fatalism, and selfishness in a way that’s totally at odds with the practice of Lincoln or King or anyone else who’s ever accomplished anything. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">America the beautiful </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But to return from the realm of instrumentality, it’s worth saying that America is a pretty awesome country. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The notion of the United States as a sweet land of liberty did not fully reflect the reality of 1939. But it wasn’t some kind of crazy cynical lie on a par with North Korea’s claim to be a democratic people’s republic. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The United States </span><em>really was</em><span> founded by a lot of religious dissenters and was genuinely a global pioneer in promoting pluralism and electoral democracy. It’s good and correct to say that the United States fell short of its ideals, but I think it’s also important to talk about the part where heroes fought to make the country live up to them and about the ways in which Americans have, through history, lived up to them. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And if you think about the recent history of the United States, there’s something blinkered about viewing the existence of racial tension and ethnic conflict as a distinctive fact of American life rather than a tragic but banal aspect of the human condition. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>People from all around the world are constantly trying to move here because the United States is a good place to live. The United States has the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/81c57de4-0c8c-402b-871f-db9346a5cee2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">highest median living standards</a><span> in the world outside of a handful of very small countries like Norway. We have probably the freest speech you’ll find anywhere. We have a robust and longstanding civic culture of integration, where the children and grandchildren of immigrants can also lay claim to being the metaphorical children of the founding fathers of the country. We landed humans on the Moon, we split the atom, we have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b458b6ab-5e94-4b68-bc8a-684632b353ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">the most Nobel Prize winners</a><span>, we developed the best Covid vaccines, we created the internet, and we’re at the leading edge of artificial intelligence. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Americans are not the absolute number one most tolerant people with regard to who we are willing to welcome as neighbors, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8b1282cb-ac2c-470a-b53b-9f6e5f7ce058?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">but we’re way up there</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is basically what schools should teach kids. Not that America is or ever was perfect, but that relative to other actually existing places, the United States has pretty consistently been a beacon of opportunity and freedom without rival. Everyone should sing the songs and pledge the pledges.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Learning from our forebears</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When I took the history of early-modern moral philosophy in college, the professor told our class that we should try not to read the authors too skeptically. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">She didn’t mean that we should accept everything they said as true and correct — she was prepared to grant that we were all smart people who understood how to read a text critically. Her view was that studying the history of philosophy was a worthwhile undertaking. But the value of the undertaking is not to go through some essays written a long time ago by guys using somewhat unfamiliar language and talking about somewhat unfamiliar questions and just dunk on them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The value is in trying to understand what these major thinkers of history brought to the table and why they’re interesting. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And I would really encourage us Democrats to build a public culture where we undertake our assessment of the great characters of American history in that spirit. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s easy to say that F.D.R.’s internment of Japanese Americans was bad and Ulysses Grant’s blind eye to corruption was bad and Andrew Jackson’s Trail of Tears was bad and Thomas Jefferson owning slaves was bad. Because all that stuff is really bad! </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s also genuinely important and interesting to understand how F.D.R. pulled the country out of the Great Depression and persuaded a largely unwilling nation to come to Europe’s aid. Jefferson wrote an incredible charter of human freedom. Jackson popularized our modern understanding of democracy. Grant saved the country. There’s nothing wrong with criticizing these figures, but it quickly becomes self-congratulatory and lame to gas yourself up compared to the heroic figures of the past just because you have conventional contemporary ethical views. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Part of constructing a paradigm of patriotic education should be making sure we have an inclusive canon of heroic figures to talk about so it’s not just a procession of white guys with a “too bad about the racism” asterisk. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it’s genuinely not hard to do this, and I think Donald Trump’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da01cf86-46e5-4a5d-85a4-c41518c269d2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Garden of American Heroes</a><span> list is a broadly reasonable gesture in that direction. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Patriotism is good. America’s destiny is inextricably tied up with the fate of liberalism around the world, and Democrats shouldn’t just pay lip service to those ideas — we should promote them in concrete ways. </p><p cuts against the Constitution and all kinds of core American values in a way that is almost too boring to discuss. But Washington Post Columnist Shadi Hamid went viral with a response in which he offered a hot take of his own: “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fdb98a27-afd8-4d92-b189-3f797e2ad9f9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Muslims shouldn’t have to assimilate to belong</a><span>.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jerusalem’s parents are immigrants who assimilated — making sure she learned English before entering preschool, for example — and she thinks it’s important that America continues to promote and celebrate assimilation. She puts a lot of weight on the evidence, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9d383fd7-d994-4a99-b2ea-09019ebfcb03?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>from Leah Boustan and others</span></a><span>, that immigrants to the United States do in fact assimilate very well. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I am on board with all of this, but a little more worried than Jerusalem is that it’s not good enough for liberals to reassure voters that assimilation happens. I think we need to do our share of the work to make sure that it happens. You can’t just opportunistically invoke successful assimilation to defend immigrants when they are under attack; you need to actively promote and celebrate America as a good society that is worth assimilating into. That means getting beyond certain progressive hangups about race and American history. That does not mean denying the existence of ugly episodes in the country’s story, but it does mean denying the claim that this ugliness defines America or that it is somehow unique to our country rather than part of a perennial pattern of ethnic conflict in human history.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My ancestors immigrated well before Jerusalem’s and did so at a time when the borders were generally more open but there was also more comfort with heavy-handed assimilation measures. Some of these went too far — I remember my grandfather telling me about kids in his heavily Hispanic community being beaten at school for speaking Spanish to each other — but I think there was something to the combination of legal openness and forceful promotion of American identity.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hamid argues for a kind of deep pluralism, insisting that the core of America’s founding is the idea that citizens never have to converge on foundational questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is something to this. Is it true that there is one God or several? If one, is Muhammad God’s prophet? Is there a second testament to the Bible? A third? These are deep, profound questions that Americans should and will disagree about forever, and Ogles is dead wrong to insist that any religion is out of bounds. But part of a liberal society is promoting a culture of liberalism. If numerically small sects such as the Amish or Hasidic Jews want to form insular, illiberal faith communities, there’s no issue there. But the influx of very large numbers of people with illiberal values is a real topic for concern. That shouldn’t be an excuse for ethnic bigotry or exclusion, but it’s certainly an argument that people who come here should embrace American (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b2b9a299-c448-42f3-9bec-027d09087392?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>or Dutch</span></a><span>) values and that those values should be promoted.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Paid subscribers can You would get terrible service, or you couldn’t get service at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So that meant that iPhone adoption varied according to the availability of the AT&T service network, which Caitlin Myers and Hooper think they can use to do sort of a causal analysis of the iPhone’s impact.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They say the diffusion of the iPhone explains 33 to 52% of the decline in the general fertility rate among women aged 15 to 44, based on extrapolating from this county-level rollout.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s a really large effect and an interesting effort at research design. So births falling 4.5 to 8% at ages 15 to 19, and 3.2 to 6.6 at 20 to 24 in covered counties.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And, like, I think that everyone can agree the 15 to 19 number seems, like, largely straightforwardly positive. I will go ahead and say that at least the 20 to 22 number is, like, straightforwardly positive. I will grant that 23 to 24, we can have some debate. I had some people telling me, like, no, it’s bad that 23- and 24-year-olds aren’t having children. Like, I don’t know, it just kind of depends on why.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But, like, I thought that the, like, smartphone thesis seems less plausible given those age shifts. ‘Cause it’s, like, how many young people were getting that iPhone that early? That felt at the time that that was a very older-person access to, you know what I mean?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>iPhone in 2008 was quite expensive.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah. And also just, like, you wouldn’t give your kid something like that. It just is not — it felt kind of weird to me. And also, like, there was, like, of course, the birth rate was falling even before then.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And there’s, like, a very random weird thing where there’s, like, a null effect for Black women for some reason. And I just have — there’s not really an explanation for why that would be. Like, why would the iPhone not affect Black women’s fertility? Like, just seems kind of weird.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, like, I — again, like, this — I’m not an economist. I did not, like, go through this with, like, a rigorous, like, eye to detail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I would buy that, like, largely every single thing which makes it easier for people not to talk to each other and instead have fun at home alone would, like, reduce fertility rate because it will reduce partnering. And so, like, that has that effect.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like, if you’re just, like, not going to a party and you’re staying at home and watching TV, that necessarily means you’re not having sex either. And so you’re not gonna have a kid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And so, like, that all, like, makes sense to me as, like, a broader story here. But, like, I just think it’s really interesting to think about the U.S. in the context of the rest of the world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like, the iPhone has spread, or smartphones have spread, basically universally at this point. And yet you still see, like, large variations in birth rates, even if you do see kind of, like, a large-scale decline in most countries. But the fact that there is difference indicates to me that, like, technology is interacting with culture in some way that is, I think, right now, still kind of unexplained.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>So I tried to develop a sophisticated methodological critique of this paper.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>No dice?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>No, no. I think it may just be wrong.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Oh, really? Why?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I mean, the problem is that…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Oh yeah, there’s also a porn — one of the, part of the…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Well, so they’ve tried to bolster it with this porn thing. But the question of where AT&T coverage existed during this time period is not a random subsample of the United States, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span> T&T is a big company. They can count. And so they made sure that their network is really good in the Boston-Washington corridor, all across the Pacific Coast, all throughout Florida, in the Texas Triangle, in the Chicago-Milwaukee Great Lakes population center.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And then it’s very spotty in rural America. You know, they kind of got to it late. They — depending on how close you were to cities. There’s a part of rural Texas that’s just between the big cities, and it has coverage. Also, AT&T as a company is headquartered in Texas, so their coverage there is better than elsewhere.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The authors of this paper are aware of this, that it could just be an urban-rural split. And they’re doing a lot of math to try to counteract this. I think there’s always a question when you deal with that kind of thing of, “Is it working?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Because there’s a million different papers which claim to show that there’s a large causal impact of — sometimes it’s NAFTA, sometimes it’s opioids — on voting for Republicans. But these are all just different ways of reiterating that Ohio swung a lot to the right during a specific 10-year period. Because, like, a lot of different things happened in Ohio during that span of time. And it’s — it’s just challenging.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>It’s difficult. It’s difficult to do this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>It’s a hard problem because you can’t say what is co-correlating with what.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They show that, you know, as people get smartphones, they access internet porn more. So that’s, like, a plausible hypothesis. But then, as you say, why would early — early iPhone adoption was not concentrated among teenagers, right? Like, that’s not true. So, what are we really getting at here?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think — and the effect size that they find is so big, right? And it doesn’t — that, you know, these things pick up because, like, it sounds true that smartphones have led to, like, less coupling and maybe less sex and maybe fewer babies, but, like, 50% of the…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>It’d be kind of incredible if it was true.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Right. Like, that’s just — that’s a lot. And I don’t know, man. You know, it’s kind of, like, you know, it makes the paper more interesting if you have these kind of high-end impacts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I did want to say, in the teen question, though, it’s not so much — I mean, the impact is negative across the age spectrum, which is different from — you know, you might think, I mean, when I was a teen, there was a lot of, like, anti-teen pregnancy messaging. And I took it at the time, at least, that, like, the goal of that messaging was to, like, shift people’s fertility plans forward. If that messaging caused a large decline in the teen birth rate and a small decline in the 20-something birth rate and still a decline in 30-somethings, you would say, “OK, something has gone wrong with them.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Like, well, there’s more births in the 30 range now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>There are, but — but they’re saying that their estimate of the causal impact of the iPhone is negative across the entire spectrum, but concentrated in teens, which is different from saying, you know, it just, like, shifted people, right? Because we do see that shift happening, which is, you know, fertility treatments and different life plans, so on and so forth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So they’re not — They are saying that the iPhone is just moving you uniformly negative, even if it’s concentrated among teenagers. But I don’t know.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>I always have a hard time with these papers, because I’m just, like, “Yeah, it probably seems good if people spend less time on their smartphones.” Like, just, like, I’m just gonna go ahead and say, like, that seems correct.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>You’ve become a weird phone abstentionist.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah, I have my — but I do think that, like, it’s fine to be, like, “I think iPhones or smartphones in general are, like, bad for you” without having to, like, buy these, like, really big stories about how they’re causing, like, every problem in the universe. So I’m just, like, you know, I just, like…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think this often gets cast between, like, you’re, like, a pro-smartphone, like, Taylor Lorenz, believes it’s caused all the benefits of all humanity to accrue to people who get these devices, versus, like, the Jonathan Haidts where, like, it’s causing every single problem known to man.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And I’m, like, you know, I’m gonna say this: Seems bad in general but has some positives in some cases. And, like, if everyone used it less, that seems like it would be largely good.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I just wonder with some of this stuff, you know, I think there’s a theory that the printing press, like, caused Protestantism, which in turn caused the Thirty Years’ War. And so, all these people died. So that’s bad.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the other hand, a lot of important long-term benefits accrued from the printing press. On the third hand, if your takeaway from, like, the downsides of the printing press was, like, “We shouldn’t have books in our house,” that actually wouldn’t shelter you from the Thirty Years’ War at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>No, for sure. But I just mean, like, I think that there are individual harms to being on the smartphone a lot. Like, I don’t know, like, I just watch parents on their phones next to their children. I’m, like, that seems bad all the time. Like, you know?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Yeah, that’s me. You can find me doing that all the time. No, I agree.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>As a childless adult, I’m judging.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I’m just saying, right. I mean, I’m just saying that I think, in the phones discourse, we’re not always really distinguishing clearly between what are we saying are, like, individualized harms and, like, downstream negative consequences.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Because I’m in — I mean, on the one level, yes, clearly, I think almost everybody at the margin is, like, on their phone — myself included — is on their phone a little bit too much and should, like, talk to somebody or exercise or fucking go to sleep or something like that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But there’s also this question of the macro impact on society, right? Of shifting to a world in which we are getting all this, like, app-based communication. People are dating differently. We talked about one thing, the media — like, you changing your media consumption habits won’t change the fact that The Media has been fundamentally altered by smartphones and social media, and we’re not gonna uninvent it, so...</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>I actually think that, you know — this is hot take prediction coming in. I think that, like, reduced smartphone use and, like, increased use of more dumb phone technology is gonna become, like, a classic signifier. Yeah. This is my take.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>So I’ll be — I’ll be a working class champion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>You will be a working class champion scrolling on Twitter on your deathbed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Just tweeting, tweeting all the time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Well, if you enjoyed this conversation, please subscribe to </span><em><span>The Argument</span></em><span>. Tell your friends about it. Like, comment, and have a happy July 4th.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Happy birthday, America. We’re patriots now.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table </span><span>The Court has now stripped regulatory agencies of their independence from Trump’s whims and corrupt practices. Even for an agency created by Congress with a specific mandate and responsibilities, </span><span>Trump is</span><span> now</span><span> free to direct that agency to do something completely different</span><span>,</span><span> to fire any civil servants who don’t do whatever he wants</span><span>, or to completely gut it so that it is unable to serve its function</span><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Notice that I said that </span><em>Trump</em><span> has been given dictatorial power. There have been many comments to the effect that a future Democratic president could make extensive use of these new powers, but this Court is utterly partisan</span><span>. T</span><span>he </span><span>moment</span><span> a Democrat takes office, it will instantly decide that he or she has almost no discretionary power.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Various MAGA-adjacent parties, along with willfully blind centrists, are trying to sweep this ruling under the rug, hoping that the public doesn’t understand its meaning. In fact, even I am startled that </span><span>the </span><em>Wall Street Journal,</em><span> whose reporting is normally excellent, barely mentions this astonishing act of Trump empowerment in its news section. </span><span>Instead, it has posted only a misleading editorial, repeating the tendentious legal arguments of the Roberts radicals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But you don’t have to take my word for how much this </span><span>travesty </span><span>matters. As the screenshot at the top of this post shows, the wannabe dictator is fully aware of how much the </span><span>Roberts </span><span>Court has undermined democracy</span><span> in his favor. A</span><span>nd he’s celebrating.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What I want to do in today’s post is enlarge on why </span><em>Slaughter</em><span> matters — and just how bad it is.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, this decision is (almost) all about enabling corruption. Yes, there are ideological and policy aspects. But this Court decision is fundamentally about empowering Trump, not the presidency in general. And we know who and what Trump is. The normally soft-spoken </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1c1ecf2b-03ec-416c-b0a1-3bfd2b3a5b25?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Jared Bernstein</a><span> says it clearly:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[G]iving </span><em><span>this</span></em><span> president such carte blanche is crazy. Name one firing or removal he’s made or attempted to make that was motivated by anything other than personal retribution, prejudice (it is not a coincidence that Lisa Cook is a Black woman), or personal greed.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Court’s decision effectively eliminates government by professional civil servants who do their best to implement the law with government by henchmen and lackeys who will do whatever Dear Leader wants. And what he wants depends, above all, on who is most willing and able to enrich him, his family, and his cronies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In my </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/687759da-0cf9-4028-b8f0-091da7fea3f9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>conversation with Lisa Graves</span></a><span> posted yesterday, she gave the example of Jeff Yass, a billionaire who clearly purchased a complete reversal of Trump’s position on TikTok. The same has been true, on an even bigger scale, for policy toward cryptocurrency — which Trump denounced until it became clear that crypto was a way for corporations and super-rich individuals to funnel billions of dollars directly to him and his family.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Second, the Court’s sort-of carve-out for the Federal Reserve — for which, for the moment, the Court has preserved some of the protections the whole government had until now — looks even more hypocritical once we recognize the centrality of the issue of corruption.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As many people have noted, there is no conceivable argument under which the independence of monetary policy is somehow more sacred than the independence of regulation of critical areas such as antitrust policy, environmental policy, food and drug standards, and air safety.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Beyond that, Fed policy stands out as an arena in which the scope for corruption is relatively limited. While the Fed does play a role as a financial regulator, its key job is interest rate policy — and that’s basically choosing the setting on a single dial, with no room for favoritism. When the Fed raises rates, it raises rates for everyone, when it cuts rates it cuts them for everyone, with no way to exempt Trump cronies from rate hikes or give them selective rate cuts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By contrast, the Federal Trade Commission can selectively reward some corporations by granting approval for the mergers they want while selectively punishing some corporations by </span><em><span>denying </span></em><span>approval for mergers. The Environmental Protection Agency can waive pollution regulations for some companies while enforcing them for others. And so on. And we know exactly what will determine which companies get favored treatment: It will be all about who greases Trump’s palm and puffs up his ego.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why, then, give the Fed special treatment? Probably because the Court feared the market reaction if it allowed Trump to take immediate control. The Wall Street Journal editorial openly acknowledged this concern, explaining the carve-out for the Fed by saying: “</span><em><span>the Chief and Justice Kavanaugh made the pragmatic judgment that they simply don’t trust Mr. Trump to run monetary policy.” </span></em><span>But the last time I looked at the Constitution there wasn’t a special “unless it adversely affects the stock market” clause. Evidently, the Journal editorial board thinks it is only the little people who will be victims of Trump’s destruction of America’s regulatory institutions, while those who have big stock portfolios will be A-okay.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And they might be right given the trends in our economy. </span><span>A headline in yesterday’s </span><em>Journal</em><span>:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdaf5f7f-d4f5-4074-9ed6-ae2fe6fd5796?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">UCG</a><span>/Contributor via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I don’t feel like celebrating America’s 250th anniversary, and the fact that I don’t is pissing me off.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The semiquincentennial is the anniversary of a country that, whatever else is true of it, has functioned for a quarter millennium as a bet that people who show up with nothing can build something. Donald Trump and Trumpism have spent the past year and a half turning the anniversary into a branding exercise to further the inherently unpatriotic MAGA project.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You’d be forgiven for not following the inside baseball of the country’s 250th, because a nonpartisan anniversary should not be something to keep an eye on. </span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Congress set up the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d5386454-60a1-4210-b06f-6d0c67c53db6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission</span></a><span> — the body behind America250 — way back in 2016. It included 16 private citizens, four senators, and four House members, with the congressional seats split evenly by party; George W. Bush and Barack Obama later signed on as honorary co-chairs. Then, nine days into his second term, Trump signed an</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dac44165-fd01-4d4e-9462-6bf5a3947f3d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span> executive order</span></a><span> creating a second, competing anniversary program. He installed himself as chair and directed the Interior Department to treat Freedom 250 as the “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b813b0d6-653b-48ca-a916-ee656b7216f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>primary branding</span></a><span>” for the whole affair, redirecting at least</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/44a61c07-e21a-4679-ab21-b5264471a198?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span> $10 million</span></a><span> in funds Congress had appropriated for the nonpartisan commission.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unlike America250, Freedom 250 doesn’t </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7ea98c5e-d507-403d-be89-eeac0f86dd7e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>disclose its donors</span></a><span> online and has been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9385998d-b0df-4187-847b-8178ed3e53c5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>selling access by the tier</span></a><span>. Half a million dollars buys V.I.P. seating at every event, $1 million buys a private reception with the president and what the group calls a “historic photo opportunity,” while $2.5 million buys a speaking slot at a July 4 event in D.C.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When several of the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/44a61c07-e21a-4679-ab21-b5264471a198?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>musical acts</span></a><span> booked for the marquee concert pulled out rather than be associated with it, the president threatened to cancel the concerts instead of recruit new performers. He </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5b60f0e9-e1c1-45f1-b030-cfe1716f7972?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>said he would hold</span></a><span> “a giant MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN RALLY” and dismissed the lineup as “overpriced singers, who nobody wants to hear.” He has made himself the headliner.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All this is par for the course from a president who has time and time again put himself before the country he is meant to serve. And it isn’t really his bummer celebration that is getting to me; I’m mostly sad that Americans’ attitude toward America has soured under the president’s shameful leadership.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Surveys from major polling organizations have found that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1863700c-b148-4813-80fe-a3eab06b2d73?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>national pride is falling</span></a><span> while pessimism is rising, and young Americans especially are rejecting displays of patriotism. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/856b430b-6fea-417c-a4db-9d46f5aa1b50?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Gallup</span></a><span> found that more than three quarters of Americans believe that the nation’s founders would be disappointed by the country today. The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1bf5e3ab-5278-4b57-abf0-062c4ef7f0bf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Public Religion Research Institute</span></a><span> found that Americans are both less patriotic and less sure of what patriotism means.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The argument that it feels improper to celebrate America right now is not a fringe take, especially on the left. But this is still a country worth celebrating, and surrendering patriotism to Trump’s version of it lets him and his movement define what the nation stands for. Once Americans do that, we give up on this country, and any hope of restoring the project of independence and freedom is dead. These are ideals I believe are worth fighting for.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=159185&post_id=203609198&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=false&r=4wxxxa&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoyOTcxOTYwMzAsInBvc3RfaWQiOjIwMzYwOTE5OCwiaWF0IjoxNzgyOTAwMzk2LCJleHAiOjE3ODU0OTIzOTYsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0xNTkxODUiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0._ER0ZwPhZlxKiD3mGU6lT0e2I1VyHXXVqinMRMQd4GU","text":"Share","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=159185&post_id=203609198&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=false&r=4wxxxa&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoyOTcxOTYwMzAsInBvc3RfaWQiOjIwMzYwOTE5OCwiaWF0IjoxNzgyOTAwMzk2LCJleHAiOjE3ODU0OTIzOTYsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0xNTkxODUiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0._ER0ZwPhZlxKiD3mGU6lT0e2I1VyHXXVqinMRMQd4GU" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #04B2A5;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Share</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My grandmother and her parents came to the United States after the Holocaust destroyed their lives in Poland. This was the country that took them in and allowed them to rebuild. That opportunity made them, and now me, patriots.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My family’s story is not unique; it is the most common story in this country. I grew up in Colorado, where more than </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c1ec82af-93c2-4cdc-914b-ac81e8360717?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>80,000 refugees</span></a><span> have resettled and rebuilt since 1980, becoming homeowners, small-business owners, taxpayers, voters, and neighbors. This possibility is the result of a promise made by this country.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That promise is being broken right now, and it is up to those of us who believe in it to hold this administration accountable. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a3bc7c79-b1ea-409d-a9f8-afc00810158b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Colorado Public Radio reported</span></a><span> in March on a 30-year-old Afghan man who mapped satellite data for the U.S.-backed government in Kabul before the Taliban retook the country in 2021. After the takeover, he fled to Iran, found a Denver nonprofit through a cold LinkedIn message, and was eventually granted humanitarian parole into Colorado in June 2023, where he built a </span><span>small business detailing cars.</span><span> He has done everything by the book, but his pathway to citizenship is no clearer. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In December 2025, after Trump paused asylum processing, he got a notice to appear at an ICE check-in. He was allowed to leave after the appointment, but his case is still unresolved and could take years. He’s one of roughly 5,000 people in Colorado who are currently stuck in that kind of limbo, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a3bc7c79-b1ea-409d-a9f8-afc00810158b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Colorado Public Radio</a><span> reports. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Eighty years separate my family’s welcome from his delayed one, but both stories unfold under the same flag. His treatment, which is owned entirely by this administration, is not a verdict on the country that made the original promise.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I understand the argument that it is naive, and perhaps dishonest, to wave a flag or call yourself a patriot when the people running the government have made patriotism feel synonymous with loyalty to them. I understand, too, the feeling that it is impossible to celebrate a country that produced these current conditions. Watching the anniversary get taken over and monetized by the man breaking each of the country’s promises makes the idea of flying a flag feel like agreeing with him.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But ceding the flag, the word “patriot,” and this anniversary to Trump and the movement built around him is a forfeit. It only gives him the one thing he actually wants, which is sole custody of what it means to love this country.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Patriotism and nationalism aren’t synonyms. One is loyalty to a place and to the standard it set for itself, including the duty to say where it’s fallen short. The other is loyalty to a brand, an in-group, and a leader who just happens to be holding the flag. The administration usurping “America’s birthday” does not have a stronger claim to loving this country than the people walking away from it do. But those people who walk away are the ones who will be at fault for handing the country over to the thing they claim to hate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is plenty to be ashamed of in American history. There was slavery and the violent displacement of Native nations, the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d5cc358-1a06-4ced-92b2-aa8d9f00bce7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>incarceration of roughly 120,000 Japanese Americans</span></a><span> without trial during World War II, and the fact that we didn’t federally guarantee Black Americans the vote nationwide until the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed4d6a94-179d-4e5f-a778-d383edd54d97?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Voting Rights Act of 1965</span></a><span>. </span><span>That history is something to remember and remark on, but this country also has a Constitution flexible enough to be amended 27 times, including amendments that corrected some of its worst sins; it has won civil rights fights at the ballot box and in court, not only in the streets; and it still naturalizes hundreds of thousands of new citizens almost every year — people who, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8ab503dc-a89d-4477-b70b-8c5729d50c5a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">by most measures</a><span>, describe themselves as more patriotic than those born here. One new citizen in D.C. this winter told </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/33252666-7865-41ae-9b22-2284915e6e72?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>National Public Radio</span></a><span> that even before she naturalized, she had become an American “in my mind and my heart.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So I am sad that 250 years — the only major milestone that I can count on being around for — is one I am not in the mood to celebrate. This is a country worth keeping, and the people who actually believe in the experiment and its unfinished promise are the ones who can save it from a movement that has never shown much interest in any of that. I’m proud to believe in the democratic experiment and grateful to have been born in a country that has given me educational, social, and career opportunities that seem like a distant dream to people all over the world. And I want those opportunities not only to survive but to expand during the country’s 250th year and every year after Trump has become a fading stain on our democracy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Walking away does not punish Trump. It just leaves him holding the flag in victory, which is the one outcome he can’t achieve on his own. I’m not giving him mine, even though I’m angry that he crashed the party.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" 26px;font-size: 16px;">The basic idea was twofold:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">AI can inject lots of information into debates in real time, in order to bring them back to reality and correct misinformation.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">AI is trained on a sample of writing from Democrats AND Republicans, so it tends to be more moderate than the typical human being in a polarized society.</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I called depolarizing AI “Digital Cronkite”, because it could be a modern version of Walter Cronkite’s moderate voice of authority on broadcast television in the mid 20th century. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My post cited some papers in support of the thesis. Here’s one more. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6ee8b585-227b-42f4-abfd-9a0638ac73bd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Conlon and Schwardmann (2026)</a><span> set out to study the phenomenon of “AI sycophancy” — i.e., AI telling people what they want to hear. Sycophancy is a well-documented phenomenon — if you tell AI that bears ride bikes, it’s disturbingly likely to agree. Some people are naturally afraid that sycophancy will increase political polarization, by reinforcing people’s political beliefs. If AI tells Democrats “Yes, Republicans are bad and you’re right about everything,” and if it tells Republicans “Yes, Democrats are bad and you’re right about everything,” that could seemingly entrench polarization by turning every human-AI conversation into a little echo chamber. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Conlon and Schwardmann found that AI does the exact opposite of this! From their abstract:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Our experiment involves 1,500 participants in 30 decision environments spanning core domains in economics and the social sciences…[W]e find that AI advice </span><strong>depolarizes choices on average</strong><span>, moving participants away from their initial leanings. This depolarization arises despite the LLM being measurably sycophantic: it disproportionately offers considerations that support users’ initial leanings and uses agreeable and flattering language. Depolarization occurs across moral and non-moral, objective and subjective, strategic and non-strategic, and complex and simple tasks. Increasing sycophancy weakens depolarization, showing that sycophancy is behaviorally relevant, even if it is generally outweighed by the informativeness of AI advice. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The authors go with the “substantive information” theory of AI depolarization, and they find some evidence to support it: </p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why then does our baseline LLM depolarize choices, despite being sycophantic? One hypothesis is that it combines its agreeable framing with enough substantive information to counteract sycophancy’s polarizing force. Several facts corroborate this interpretation. First, in objective tasks, interacting with the baseline AI improves accuracy by 0.12 standard deviations (p < 0.05)…In contrast, we find no evidence that extra deliberation time, reactance, noise, or ceiling effects drive our results.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Interestingly, Conlon and Schwardmann don’t think about what seems to me to be the most obvious reason for AI depolarization — i.e., that AI is trained on the average of society, and thus is the ultimate Moderate Normie. That’s something worth following up on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But whatever the reason, this is another piece of evidence in favor of the Digital Cronkite thesis. You should probably be a little more optimistic about AI’s effect on human politics. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">3. A bad argument from a good economist about AI risk</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anthropic recently </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5186d24a-3914-4eff-b986-e6b06d2f1ae9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">hired Chad Jones</a><span>, my favorite growth theorist. That’s great news, both for Chad and for Anthropic! But </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cb97f646-238f-49e8-af87-9a8810b43ad8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a Financial Times article</a><span> about the hire catches Chad saying some highly questionable things about existential AI risk in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/53b90ae2-9753-41a5-9993-4b35ac3748a7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a working paper back in 2023</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What is the price of this amazing change in living standards? Recall that we would face a flow probability of existential risk of 1% per year for 40 years, so the probability we survive this A.I. explosion is exp(−.01 × 40) ≈ 0.67. In other words, with log utility it is optimal to take a 1 in 3 chance of ending human existence in exchange for a 2/3 chance of dramatically raising living standards by a factor of 55.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Chad’s point here is not that we should be blasé about the existential risk from AI. His purpose in the paper is to compare different utility functions and show how our attitude toward existential risk can change a lot depending on risk aversion. But I still don’t like his calculation here.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main reason is that Chad </span><strong>sets the utility of human extinction equal to zero</strong><span>. This </span><em>isn’t </em><span>actually log utility. Log utility is just u(c) = ln(c), where c is consumption. If you consume nothing at all, then ln(c) = ln(0) = -∞. In other words, if you take log utility seriously, then death is infinitely bad.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That presents a problem for economic models, since it means that even the slightest chance of death is so scary — scarier even than a bear on a bicycle — that humans would do basically </span><em>anything</em><span> to avoid it. That obviously isn’t realistic. So instead, economists using log utility typically model it with a fudge factor. One option is to just set u=0. This is the assumption that if you’re dead, you’re not getting any utility from anything, so your utility should just be zero forever. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s what Chad Jones is doing in this paper, and it’s that choice that drives his result. But it’s a highly dubious assumption. Recall that ln(1) = 0. So this means that if you assume u(extinction) = 0, you’re saying that “humanity going extinct” is no worse than “humanity existing for all eternity at some baseline level of consumption”. That doesn’t sound realistic to me. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A better choice — which is what some economists do — is to set the utility of death equal to some constant, and then try to calibrate that constant against data on risky behavior. The constant wouldn’t be zero, and it would greatly alter Chad’s calculations on how much benefit we’d need from AI in order to accept existential risk. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But even here, we have to be cautious. Human extinction is not the same as an individual’s death. A lot of people would probably accept a lot less risk if they knew they were risking the lives of their families, friends, countrymen, and fellow human beings, than if they were only risking their own life. So you have to be very careful when looking at how much people care about the risk of the whole species dying. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Chad was not being careful here. I know this was 2023, before existential risk seemed like a serious thing to people outside the AI industry. But now that he’s at Anthropic, he should be more circumspect about these things. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">4. Millennials are doing better than Boomers (but are more unequal)</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">During the 2010s, there was a pretty common narrative that economic progress had stalled in America, and that the Millennial generation had been screwed over. You still hear a few progressives argue this, but in general this narrative has been in retreat as new data has come in. As the Millennials have eased into middle age, it has become apparent that like every generation before them, they have experienced substantial economic progress. So government is helping produce upward mobility for the poor. This is a big government success story. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the narrative that Millennials are falling behind, and that the Boomers screwed their children over, just doesn’t hold up in the income data. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">5.
